vignette:
The Weight of Numbers

Marcus is a 35-year-old Filipino accountant who sits across from his therapist with his hands folded neatly in his lap, a posture that suggests someone who has spent years trying to take up as little space as possible. He speaks carefully, measuring his words the way he measures figures in a spreadsheet — with precision, and with the quiet terror of finding something that doesn't balance.

Seven years ago, Marcus was working as a junior financial analyst in Manila when he became inadvertently entangled in a corruption investigation involving a government contractor. He had flagged irregularities in the accounts — the right thing to do, he still tells himself, though he no longer says it with any conviction. Before the matter could reach his superiors through proper channels, he was taken. Three men came to his apartment on a Tuesday evening. He remembers the specific day because he had been watching a football match, and the sound of the crowd was the last ordinary thing he heard for what turned out to be eleven days.

What happened during those eleven days Marcus describes only in fragments, and only when the silence in the room feels safe enough. He was held in a concrete room with no windows. He was beaten systematically. There were burns. There were periods of forced sleeplessness that he says felt worse than the physical pain — a kind of dissolution of the self that he still struggles to name. He was released without explanation, left outside a hospital with no memory of how he got there.

He emigrated to Australia two years later, sponsored by a cousin in Melbourne, and retrained as an accountant. On paper, this chapter reads as recovery — new country, stable profession, a brief marriage to a woman he describes as kind but ultimately unable to reach him. The divorce was finalised eighteen months ago. She had told him, gently and then not so gently, that she felt she was living with someone who was always waiting for something terrible to happen.

She was not wrong. Marcus moves through his days in a state of low-grade vigilance that exhausts him. At work, he is meticulous and well-regarded, but he keeps his office door locked from the inside and has positioned his desk so that his back is never to the entrance. When a colleague raises their voice in a meeting — even in laughter — Marcus feels his body flood with something cold and electric. He does not call it fear. He calls it being careful.

He sleeps poorly. When he does sleep, he often wakes at three or four in the morning with his heart hammering, the smell of concrete and cigarette smoke somehow present in a room where neither exists. He has not told anyone at work about what happened to him. He has not told his family in the Philippines, who believe he left for better opportunities. He carries the story alone, which has made him, he says quietly, very tired.

The numbers help. There is something about the internal logic of accounting — the way debits must equal credits, the way every entry has a corresponding entry — that gives Marcus a framework the rest of his life refuses to provide. He works long hours, often staying until the office building empties, because the walk home in the dark is something he still has to brace himself for each evening. He scans faces on the tram. He takes note of exits.

He came to therapy, he explains, not because he believes it will help, but because his GP told him his blood pressure was too high for a man his age and asked if he was under stress. He said yes, which was the first honest answer he had given anyone in years. He is not sure what he is hoping for. He thinks perhaps he is hoping to find out whether the person who watched that football match on a Tuesday evening still exists somewhere, or whether those eleven days simply erased him.

He unfolds his hands. He folds them again.
